the marine redox evolution at Ganxi was mainly controlled by the interplay between marine productivity and terrigenous weathering inputs, and the latter was the primary driver of the global transition from euxinic (oxygen-deficient) to ferruginous (iron-rich) oceanic conditions during the latest Changhsingian.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the marine redox conditions during the latest Wuchiapinghan to earliest Induan interval in South China were mainly controlled by the interactions among the oceanic productivity, terrigenous inputs, and volcanism.

the LPME was preceded by a protracted euxinic episode that lasted for ~2.5 Myr (from the late Wuchiapingian through the early Changhsingia), which was followed by a ~2.5-Myr-long ferruginous episode spanning the LPME through the early Triassic.

the marine redox conditions during the PTB transition in South China were controlled by the combined effects of enhanced marine productivity (upwelling) and elevated terrestrial weathering fluxes (volcanism) in a carbonate-ramps setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the redox transition was not a global phenomenon, and the marine redox conditions at Ganxi were more sensitive to local factors (e.g., enhanced terrigenous inputs) than global factors (e.g. volcanism).
the marine redox evolution at Ganxi was largely controlled by oceanographic changes, with a minor contribution from enhanced volcanic inputs.

the marine redox evolution across the PTB in the South China region was not only controlled by contemporaneous global changes in oceanic circulation but also by the interplay of regional factors such as marine productivity, weathering, and volcanism.
